questions.q: What is the inciting incident in "Mother's Day" and why does it occur at the specific moment it does in the play's timeline?
questions.a: The inciting incident is the personality swap between Mrs. Pearson and Mrs. Fitzgerald, performed via a spell ("Arshtatta dum—arshtatta lam—arshtatta lamdumbona") at the moment Mrs. Pearson admits she doesn't know how to confront her family. A wrong answer (e.g., "Doris entering" or "George coming home") reveals the student confuses the *first event of rising action* with the *catalyst that disrupts equilibrium*. The swap must happen before any family member appears because it creates the new reality that drives all subsequent conflict.

questions.q: Explain how the play's one-act structure (continuous time, single setting) amplifies the dramatic tension compared to a multi-act version with time jumps.
questions.a: The single living-room setting and unbroken afternoon compress all confrontations into one relentless sequence: Doris (tea/ironing), Cyril (mending/club), George (stout/club humiliation), then the collective resolution. No scene changes or time gaps allow characters to "cool off" — each family member walks into the escalating pressure cooker. A wrong answer focusing only on "unity of time" misses the *causal chain*: Cyril hears Doris's account, George enters seeing Doris's tears, Mrs. Fitzgerald arrives mid-crisis. The structure forces immediate repercussions.

questions.q: Map the three confrontations (Doris, Cyril, George) onto the rising action curve. Which confrontation marks the turning point toward climax and why?
questions.a: Doris (first) establishes the new dynamic; Cyril (second) expands it to include male privilege and labor; George (third) is the turning point because it publicly exposes the father's fragility ("Pompy-ompy Pearson") and shifts power irrevocably. A wrong answer treating all three as equal reveals failure to see *escalation*: George's humiliation is the climax because it breaks the patriarchal authority that underpinned the family's exploitation of Mrs. Pearson. The club revelation ("They call you Pompy-ompy Pearson") is the point of no return.

questions.q: Analyze how the off-stage characters (Charlie Spence, the club members, the "greyhound races") function structurally. What would be lost if they appeared on stage?
questions.a: Off-stage characters expand the play's social world without diluting focus on the nuclear family. Charlie Spence represents Doris's shallow romantic life; the club members externalize George's deluded self-image; the races symbolize Cyril's escapism. Their absence keeps the stage a pressure chamber — if they appeared, the play would become social realism rather than concentrated domestic satire. A wrong answer ("saves actors/cost") misses the *structural economy*: off-stage forces are invoked only when the on-stage characters weaponize them (e.g., Mrs. Pearson citing the club's mockery to destroy George's authority).

questions.q: Evaluate whether the resolution (the second swap and the family rummy game) is earned or contrived. Support your judgment with structural evidence.
questions.a: The resolution is *earned* because the second swap occurs only after Mrs. Fitzgerald (as Mrs. Pearson) insists "that's enough" — acknowledging the lesson has limits. The rummy game isn't a magical fix; it's a negotiated new contract: "you children could get the supper ready while I have a talk with your father." Structurally, the play returns to the opening situation (tea, cards, family together) but with inverted power dynamics. A wrong answer calling it "too easy" ignores that the *threat* of Mrs. Pearson's firmness ("a firm hand") is what sustains the change — the structure ends on a conditional equilibrium, not a fairy-tale ending.

questions.q: Create a one-paragraph "deleted scene" set the next morning that demonstrates whether the structural change in family dynamics holds. Use only dialogue and stage directions.
questions.a: A strong answer shows the new norms operating without Mrs. Fitzgerald's presence: e.g., George making his own tea, Doris ironing her own silk, Cyril mending his clothes, Mrs. Pearson reading a newspaper. Weak answers revert to old patterns (Mrs. Pearson serving) or introduce new magic — revealing the student hasn't internalized that the structure's resolution *replaced* supernatural intervention with behavioral change. The test: does the scene prove the "firm hand" works without the spell?

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Plot and narrative structure in drama?
questions.a: Students often treat the body-swap as mere fantasy plot device rather than a *structural metaphor* for psychological breakthrough.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently map the five-act structural elements onto the one-act play "Mother's Day," identify the inciting incident (the personality swap), trace how rising action builds through three confrontations (Doris, Cyril, George), explain the climax (George's public humiliation), and articulate how the resolution restores.
